eal.newcomerCriteria.AO|Angola: Not established from the sources consulted. Angola's Lei de Bases do Sistema de Educação e Ensino (Lei 17/16, art. 16) requires teaching to be delivered in Portuguese and permits Angola's other languages to be used only as a complement and instrument of learning, and the law creates no newcomer or second-language pupil category, leaving the regime of access to and attendance at schools by foreign citizens to be defined in a separate instrument that the law does not name. UNICEF's 2016 study of the impact of language policy and practice on children's learning in Angola records no such designation either; its nearest equivalent is a ministry study of the language fluency of mobile and migrating populations. A systematic sweep of lex.ao in September 2026 — 7,286 diplomas, the full text of 4,835 covering 2020 to 2026 and 2,451 document pages fetched individually for 2016 to 2019 — found exactly one instrument ever enacted under art. 107(3): Decreto Presidencial 276/19, whose preamble cites "o n.º 3 do artigo 107.º" of Lei 17/16, which wrote nothing on foreign citizens and was revoked by Decreto Presidencial 162/23. The deferral is unfilled rather than unfound.
eal.newcomerCriteria.KP|North Korea: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for the DPRK, read in full, contains no occurrence of "minority", "ethnic", "foreign", "refugee", "migrant" or "language of instruction" anywhere in the document; its entire inclusion content concerns disability, and "Korean" appears only in institution names. The 2016 Socialist Constitution's language provisions (Arts. 54 and 159) concern protecting the Korean language and the language of court proceedings, not schooling. Searched: PEER DPRK inclusion profile, Constitute Project text of the Socialist Constitution, UNESCO UIS country pages (uis.unesco.org/en/country/kp redirects to a generic landing page and does not resolve to a DPRK profile), and UNESDOC. Not asserted either way. Both education laws have since been read in full from the ROK 통일법제 database: the Education Law (교육법, SPA Presidium Decree 847 of 1999, as amended to 2015) and the General Education Law (보통교육법, Decree 1355 of 2011, as amended to 2015). Across both, 외국인, 언어, 조선어, 소수, 귀국, 재외, 편입 and 전학 return zero occurrences; 외국 appears once, as 외국어, a school subject. The only pupil categories either law creates are the universal duty on local people's committees to identify and enrol every child of school age, and provision for children in deep mountains, remote islands and with disabilities. The single non-discrimination clause is on sex.

eal.removalCriteria.CA|New Brunswick: Not established from the sources consulted. Two of the province's own EECD documents were reached this time, through Internet Archive mirrors of the gnb.ca originals — Teaching English as an Additional Language in New Brunswick: A Guide for Educators and School Teams, and the EAL 110 and 120 curriculum — and neither sets a rule for ending an EAL designation. The curriculum places learners at a CEFR level from placement assessments taken at time of arrival and tracks progress in a language portfolio, but states no exit threshold, no time limit and no re-designation rule; there is no EAL policy in the EECD numbered policy series. On the francophone side, the CMEC Student Transfer Guide records only that French as an Additional Language courses are offered regardless of grade level, age or mother tongue. Every gnb.ca host still answers 403 to a browser User-Agent, a bare User-Agent and curl alike.
eal.removalCriteria.VE|Venezuela: Not established from the sources consulted. The 1999 Constitution recognises only two language categories in education — Castilian as the official language (art. 9) and an intercultural bilingual regime that belongs to indigenous peoples (art. 121) — and neither it nor the 2009 Ley Orgánica de Educación creates a newcomer or second-language designation that could be ended, so no exit rule, time limit or re-designation rule arises from them.

eal.achievementGap.CU|Cuba: Not established from the sources consulted for this entry — no attainment data disaggregated by home language located. If you work in this system, this is exactly the field to fill in.

eal.l2Support.EG|Egypt: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER profile records that instruction is generally delivered in Arabic at all education levels and that Article 24 of the 2014 Constitution makes the Arabic language a core subject of pre-university public and private education, with no additional-language or newcomer provision named anywhere in the profile; Human Rights Watch, reporting in December 2024, says that some of the people it interviewed described refugees and asylum seekers from non-Arabic speaking countries as discriminated against in enrolment, which affects access to public schools for populations including some 40,000 registered from Eritrea and 18,700 from Ethiopia.
eal.l2Support.IR|Iran: Not established from the sources consulted. Persian is the constitutionally required language of textbooks and instruction (Art. 15, 1989 Constitution), and the UNHCR Iran education page states refugee and undocumented children follow "the same national curriculum" as Iranian children, but no source retrieved in this session sets out a Persian-as-a-second-language provision: no entitlement, no hours, no designated staff. Searched: UNESCO PEER Iran inclusion profile (no language-support section), UNHCR Iran education page, the ADSP 2018 review of the Supreme Leader's decree (access only, silent on language), and the Center for Human Rights in Iran 2021 report on mother languages, which describes teachers in Sistan and Baluchistan teaching Persian from scratch in first grade as an unsupported local difficulty rather than a programme. Not asserted either way.

eal.l2Support.MN|Mongolia: Not established from the sources consulted. Mongolian is the constitutional official language (Art. 8) and the 2002 Law on Education as amended in 2006 "permits the use of the local language for communicating in the school environment (Art. 30.1.12)", but no source retrieved in this session sets out a Mongolian-as-a-second-language provision for Kazakh- or Tuvan-speaking pupils: no entitlement, no hours, no designated staff. Searched: UNESCO PEER Mongolia inclusion profile, the Constitute Project text of the Constitution, and the Asia-Pacific Multilingual Education Working Group Mongolia country profile at asiapacificmle.net, which returned HTTP 200 but served an empty JavaScript shell with no retrievable text. Not asserted either way.
eal.l2Support.PS|Palestine: Not established from the sources consulted. UNESCO's PEER Inclusion profile for the State of Palestine records that the Basic Law makes Arabic the official language and therefore the language of instruction in schools, and that Hebrew is learned as a second language from the third grade and English as a third language, but it describes no service for pupils who arrive without Arabic; the remedial learning plans it does describe are for low academic achievement, not for language.

eal.l1Support.LA|Laos: Not established from the sources consulted. The UNESCO PEER inclusion profile for Lao PDR contains no occurrence of "mother tongue", "bilingual" or "multilingual" anywhere in the document; its ethnic-group provision is framed entirely as access to Lao-medium schooling, with "ethnic primary and secondary schools" described as boarding-type provision for remote learners ("As of 2017, there were only 20 throughout the country") rather than as minority-language schools. The closest thing to home-language provision recorded is the recruitment of ethnic teachers to teach in their home areas. Searched: PEER Lao PDR inclusion profile in full, the UNICEF Lao PDR education page, and unicef.org's Lao community-based school readiness story (HTTP 403 to both curl and WebFetch, not usable). Not asserted either way.
eal.l1Support.MT|Malta: Not established from the sources consulted. Not retrieved, which is different from absent. migrantlearnersunit.gov.mt does not resolve from this network (curl exit 6, two attempts). meae.gov.mt does not resolve either, so the national policy PDF could not be read.

The PEER Lao PDR inclusion profile, read in full, does not use the words "bilingual" or "multilingual" at all, and the UNICEF Lao PDR education page describes school-readiness support in non-Lao-speaking villages without stating what language it is delivered in. Searched: PEER Lao PDR inclusion profile, UNICEF Lao PDR education page, unicef.org Lao community-based school readiness story (403), UNICEF Lao PDR 2023 Country Office Annual Report at unicef.org/media/152161/... eal.bilingualEducationNotes.MN|Mongolia: Not established from the sources consulted. The PEER Mongolia inclusion profile records a mother-tongue entitlement at pre-primary and primary level and a 2017 Asian Development Bank project "improving textbooks and other teaching and learning materials in the Kazakh language", but describes no programme that teaches content through two languages: no transition model, no language allocation, no named bilingual schools. Searched: PEER Mongolia inclusion profile, Constitute Project constitutional text, and the Asia-Pacific Multilingual Education Working Group country profile (JavaScript shell, no text). Mongolia was cited as an international example at Kyrgyzstan's 2024 National Forum on Multilingual Education (https://www.osce.org/hcnm/579406), but that release gives no description of what the Mongolian model is, so nothing is inferred from it. Not asserted either way.
